title: From fasting to building
hookLine: many hammer the first nail of the sukkah as Yom Kippur ends

cards: Yom Kippur is over. Stars are out. People pour out of the synagogue, dizzy with hunger, heading for bagels and orange juice.

And in some backyards, before anyone has sat down to eat, there's a strange sound: tap, tap, tap. Someone is out in the dark with a hammer and a flashlight, banging in a single nail, or setting up one pole.
Then they go inside and eat. They've started building a hut.

teach.b: The hut is a sukkah, the temporary booth for the festival of Sukkot. Leviticus sets Yom Kippur on the tenth of the month and Sukkot on the fifteenth: five days apart. The Torah says: "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days."

teach.h: FROM ONE MITZVAH TO THE NEXT.
teach.b: Rabbi Moshe Isserles, the great Ashkenazi authority, records the custom: right after Yom Kippur, begin building the sukkah, so as to go from one mitzvah to the next.
Some just hammer one nail that night, a token; others put up the whole frame. The idea behind it is old.
A psalm says of the faithful: "They go from strength to strength." Later teachers read it as a rule of life. Don't leave a gap after something holy.
When you finish one good thing, start the next while the energy is still warm. And look at the contrast. For ten days the focus was inward: judgment, books, confession, a day without food.
Now the very next act is outward and physical: wood, nails, branches, a roof you can see the stars through. The year doesn't stay in the synagogue.
The calendar itself moves the mood from awe to joy, from fasting to building.
Some readers add a gentle reason: just after Yom Kippur, a person is as clean as they'll ever be, and the first thing they do is start a home. Not a palace.
A hut with branches for a roof, begun with one nail, in the dark.

how: Many Jews begin building their sukkah on the night Yom Kippur ends, even if only by hammering one nail or setting up one pole, then finish it in the days before Sukkot.

practice: Think of something you've just finished, or will finish today, a task, a meal, a piece of work, even this lesson, and before the glow fades, choose the very first step of the next good thing and make it tiny: one nail.
If you pray, you can ask for strength to go from strength to strength.

wordCard.voice: Sukkah. The booth: the temporary hut for the festival of Sukkot, whose building begins the moment Yom Kippur ends.

carryVoice: Your line: go from strength to strength. A week of ask before the day, release the vows, dressed in white, once a year, even Nineveh, one long blast. Until tomorrow.
